newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen deregulating crude price by 1999.
newsitem.headline: China seen deregulating crude price by 1999.

text.p: China is likely to fully deregulate crude oil prices by 1999, a senior official from China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) said on Wednesday.
"Oil prices in China would likely be fully deregulated at the earliest by 1998 and the latest by 1999," Zeng Xingqiu, vice president of the state-owned producer, told Reuters in an interview.

China controls its domestic oil prices but has gradually relaxed the restrictions in recent years. Regulated prices have been allowed to rise closer to world price levels and a growing portion of China's output is now outside the control regime.
Zeng said about one-third of China's domestically produced oil is sold at international market prices.
Zeng said China's Daqing crude, which is mostly exported to Japan, is sold at around 1,320 yuan per tonne ($159 per tonne), already exceeding the price of London's benchmark Brent crude.
He added that regulated domestic crude prices are around 1,000 yuan per tonne, about 200 yuan below the price of Brent crude.
China last raised its domestic crude oil price by 86.1 yuan per tonne in December.
In the same month, China moved its diesel prices up 200 yuan to 2,190 yuan per tonne, fuel oil by 100 yuan to 1,000 yuan and gasoline by 100 yuan to 2,280 yuan.
CNPC sells over two-thirds of its crude oil to state-refiner, Sinopec.
